About: Drift Velocity — the Bias in the Average

Source

Topic
Current Electricity — drift velocity of free electrons in a metallic conductor.
Concept
A current is a statistical bias in a fast, random electron swarm — it is invisible in any single electron and lives only in the average.
Serves
Interpreting I = nAevd; distinguishing thermal speed from drift speed; mobility μ = vd/E = eτ/m as a property of the metal; the sign convention for electron flow vs conventional current.
Inquiry
With the field OFF, will switching it ON turn the electrons round to march along the wire, or leave each one looking random while the AVERAGE creeps?
Misconception
"The field makes the electrons turn and march." In fact each electron drifts about 10−18 m between collisions — less than a hundred-millionth of an atomic spacing — while its thermal speed is 1010 times the drift speed.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Watch the field-OFF swarm

The field is OFF. Every electron is fast (its thermal speed is about 1.57 × 106 m/s in copper), moves in a random direction, and rebounds off obstacles. The orange marker is the average position ⟨x⟩ of the whole swarm.

Watch it. ⟨x⟩ jitters around a fixed point and goes nowhere. Now predict what happens next.

2 · Predict — when you switch the field ON…

You are about to flip the field switch. What will you see on the canvas?

3 · Flip the switch, watch ⟨x⟩

Use the Field control in the sidebar (or press F) to switch the field ON. Watch the canvas — no single electron does anything new — and watch the graph below: ⟨x⟩ leaves its jitter and becomes a straight line.

The slope of that line is the drift velocity. The sidebar shows the slope measured from the graph next to the predicted I/(nAe) — they should agree.

4 · Vary I and r — the standard result

Now play with current and wire radius. Three things to check:

• Double the current → the drift doubles (slope doubles).
• Double the radius → area quadruples → drift is quartered.
• vd and E both move — the mobility μ = vd/E = eτ/m does not. It belongs to the copper, not to the current.

This is I = n A e vd, the NCERT result.

The tiny drift speed is the reason a torch lights instantly (the field, not the carriers, propagates near c) yet a given electron takes hours to cross a metre of wire.

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A copper wire is full of free electrons rushing about. The sim lets you switch an electric field along the wire off or on, and follows the average position ⟨x⟩ of the whole swarm on a graph. It is a way to picture what an electric current really is.

What you'll learn

  • What drift velocity vd is, and how it connects to the current I, the cross-section A and the carrier density n.
  • How to compare the drift speed with the electrons' random speed, and estimate the time to cross a wire.
  • What mobility μ is, and how to find the field E that a current needs in a wire.
The apparatus: free electrons in a copper wire, a marker for their average position, and a field you can switch.

What's on screen

  • Electrons (blue dots): a sample of the swarm in the wire. The sim follows 16 000 electrons and draws about 270.
  • ⟨x⟩ marker (orange line): the average position of all the electrons.
  • Graph (bottom): ⟨x⟩ against time for the last 8 s.
  • Drift velocity panel (sidebar): a measured and a predicted drift speed, the field E in the wire, and the mobility μ.
See itPress Play with the field OFF at the defaults, I = 1.0 A and r = 0.50 mm. Watch for: the blue dots moving fast in every direction, with the orange ⟨x⟩ marker above the wire and the graph below it.

The wire is copper, with n = 8.5 × 10²⁸ free electrons per m³ and resistivity ρ = 1.68 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. Both are fixed.

03

Each electron stays random while the average drifts

Free electrons in copper rush about at random speeds of order 10⁶ m/s (the sim uses 1.57 × 10⁶ m/s) and collide about every τ ≈ 2.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ s. With the field on, each electron gains a tiny extra velocity between collisions. The next collision randomises its direction again, so no electron is steered along the wire. What survives is a small bias that only the average shows:

vd = ⟨v⟩ = −eEτ/m
The minus sign: electrons drift against E, so the conventional current points the other way.

At the defaults the drift is 0.0935 mm/s, about 10¹⁰ times slower than the random speed (1.7 × 10¹⁰ with the sim's value). Between collisions the average advances only vdτ ≈ 2.3 × 10⁻¹⁸ m, about a hundred-millionth of the spacing between atoms. To make it visible, the sim exaggerates the drift 642 times and compresses the random speed to match.

See itSwitch the field ON at the defaults. Watch for: the dots still moving at random, while the orange ⟨x⟩ marker slides steadily left and the graph line turns straight.
04

Current equals n A e times the drift speed

Take a stretch of wire of length vdΔt. Every free electron inside it crosses the end face within Δt. That is nAvdΔt electrons, carrying charge nAvdΔt · e. Dividing by Δt gives the current:

I = n A e vd  ⇒  vd = I/(nAe)
n is the electron density, A = πr² the cross-section, e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

At the defaults, A = π(0.50 mm)² = 0.785 mm², so vd = 1.0/(8.5 × 10²⁸ × 7.85 × 10⁻⁷ × 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 9.35 × 10⁻⁵ m/s = 0.0935 mm/s. At that speed an electron needs about 3 h to travel 1 m. The sim's Measured readout is the slope of the graph line, and it settles close to this prediction within a few seconds.

See itSwitch the field ON at the defaults and read the panel. Watch for: Predicted at 0.0935 mm/s, with Measured settling near the same value.
05

The drift speed grows with I and falls with r²

Since vd = I/(nπr²), the drift speed is proportional to I and inversely proportional to r². Doubling I doubles vd. Doubling r makes the area four times larger, so vd falls to a quarter.

IrAvd
1.0 A0.50 mm0.785 mm²0.0935 mm/s
2.0 A0.50 mm0.785 mm²0.187 mm/s
1.0 A1.00 mm3.14 mm²0.0234 mm/s
1.0 A0.25 mm0.196 mm²0.374 mm/s

The same current through a thinner wire needs faster carriers: halving the radius quadruples the speed. Going from r = 0.50 mm to r = 2.00 mm cuts it sixteenfold, to 0.00584 mm/s. The graph shows it as a steeper line, because its vertical scale stays fixed.

See itSet I = 2.0 A with the field ON. Watch for: Predicted at 0.187 mm/s, twice the 0.0935 mm/s at 1.0 A, and a steeper graph line.
See itSet r = 1.00 mm at I = 1.0 A. Watch for: Predicted at 0.0234 mm/s, a quarter of the default, and a much flatter line.
06

Mobility belongs to the metal, not to the current

The field that drives the current follows from the microscopic Ohm's law, E = ρJ = ρI/A. Mobility is the drift speed per unit field:

μ = vd/E = eτ/m = 1/(ρne)
Units: (m/s) per (V/m) = m²/(V·s).

Both vd and E are proportional to J = I/A, so their ratio never changes. At the defaults E = 0.0214 V/m and vd = 0.0935 mm/s. Double I and both double. Double r and both fall to a quarter. Each time μ = 4.37 × 10⁻³ m²/(V·s). It depends only on copper's ρ and n, and it gives τ = μm/e ≈ 2.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ s.

See itSet I = 2.0 A and r = 1.00 mm with the field ON. Watch for: E at 0.0107 V/m and Predicted at 0.0467 mm/s, yet μ still reads 4.37e-3.
07

Where it matters

  • Slow carriers, instant light. A torch lights at once because the field spreads through the wire at close to the speed of light, and every carrier along it starts drifting together. No single electron has to travel from the switch to the bulb.
  • Counting carriers. A current of 1 A means 1/e ≈ 6.2 × 10¹⁸ electrons cross any section every second. The drift is slow because there are so many of them.
  • Thin wires run hotter. The same current needs a larger field in a thinner wire. At 1 A, E is 0.0214 V/m for r = 0.50 mm and 0.0856 V/m for r = 0.25 mm, so the power lost per metre, I × E, is four times larger.
  • Electron flow versus current. Electrons drift against E, so the conventional current arrow points opposite to their drift. The sim draws both.
08

Summary

In one line. The current in a wire, its size and its metal together decide how the electrons inside it move.

Key points

  • Each electron stays random. Only the average drifts, at vd = −eEτ/m.
  • I = nAevd, so vd is proportional to I/r².
  • μ = vd/E = eτ/m = 1/(ρne) is the same at every I and r.

Common mix-ups

  • "The field makes the electrons turn and march along the wire." Collisions randomise each electron. Only the average position moves.
  • "A slow drift means a torch should light after hours." The field reaches the whole circuit almost at once, so every carrier starts drifting together.
  • "The drift speed is the same all along a circuit." The current I is the same, but vd = I/(nAe) is larger where the wire is thinner.

Things to try on your own

  • Keep r = 0.50 mm and find the current that gives a drift near 0.5 mm/s.
  • Find a second pair of I and r with the same Predicted drift as the defaults.
  • At I = 1.0 A, compare E and μ for r = 0.25 mm and 2.00 mm.
